outcome.shown:
The sea had a voice that Silas knew better than his own. For forty years, the crashing waves against the jagged rocks of Cape Sorrow had been his only constant companion. Silas was the keeper of the Gray Gulp Light, a solitary sentinel standing against the grey Atlantic. His days were measured by the rhythmic turn of the brass gears in the lantern room, the cleaning of soot from the thick glass lenses, and the endless, aching silence. 

Life on the cape was routine, carved out of wind and salt. Silas liked it that way. The mainland was a noisy, complicated place he had long since abandoned. He was content with his tea, his pipe, and the company of the wheeling gulls.

That was until the Tuesday after the equinox. 

A severe autumn gale had spent the night thrashing the coast, leaving behind a world slick with spray and littered with the debris of the deep. After breakfast, Silas donned his oilskin coat and made his customary rounds of the rocky shore to salvage whatever driftwood had washed up. 

Amidst a tangle of rotting kelp and broken lobster traps, a flash of emerald green caught his eye. 

Silas knelt, his arthritic knees popping in protest, and brushed away the wet sand. It was a glass bottle, sealed tight with a thick lump of crimson wax that had long since lost its sheen. Inside, curled like a sleeping caterpillar, was a slip of heavy parchment. 

A thrill, sharp and unfamiliar, pierced through Silas’s habitual numbness. Bottle messages were the stuff of childhood fancy, old sailor yarns meant to amuse greenhorns in coastal taverns. Finding a real one was like catching a ghost by the tail.

Back in the warm, lamplit kitchen of the lighthouse, Silas set the kettle to boil. With the tip of his pocketknife, he chipped away the brittle wax, pulled the cork with a satisfying *pop*, and carefully tipped the bottle. A stale, sweetish scent of aged paper and sea air drifted out. Using a pair of tweezers, he coaxed the parchment free and laid it flat upon the scarred wooden table.

It was covered in ink that had faded to the color of rust, written in a neat, sweeping cursive. 

*To whoever pulls me from the tide,* it began. 

Silas adjusted his spectacles, his thumb tracing the edge of the paper. 

*My name is Clara. I write this from the deck of the brigantine *Albatross*, bound for the Carolinas. We are six days out of port, and the sea has grown heavy. My husband, Thomas, sits across from me, carving a wooden robin for our daughter left behind in Cornwall. The wind is shifting to the northeast. It smells of copper and coming ruin. If you are reading this, it means the sea has won, and I have only this glass vessel to carry my voice to the living world. Do not pity me; the ocean is vast and beautiful, even when it swallows you whole. Just remember that once, on a Tuesday in October, we were here.*

There was no date, save for the faded inscription in the corner: *October 14, 1884.*

Silas’s breath hitched in his throat. 1884. Forty years before he was even born. 

He stared at the words, the kettle whistling ignored on the stove until it sputtered and died. Clara. Thomas. A little girl in Cornwall waiting for a wooden robin that never arrived. For a long time, the kitchen was entirely still, save for the grandfather clock ticking off the seconds in the corner. 

Suddenly, the lighthouse around him felt different. It was no longer just a machine for warning ships away from danger. It was a monument to the lost, a permanent watcher over the watery graves of thousands like Clara and Thomas. They had passed through these very waters, perhaps seeing the very same beacon Silas tended every night, unaware of the doom waiting just over the horizon.

Silas stood up, walked to the window, and looked out at the churning, indifferent gray sea. The waves rolled on, uncaring and eternal, hiding their secrets in the dark trenches below. 

He walked back to the table, gently folding the parchment. He placed it inside a small wooden box where he kept his most precious possessions—a faded photograph of his mother, a silver pocket watch that had stopped ticking in 1912. 

That evening, as the sun dipped below the horizon and the great lamp sprang to life, sweeping its brilliant arc of safety across the black water, Silas felt a strange and profound shift. He was no longer just an old man hiding from the world. He was a keeper of memories, a warden of the ghosts who drifted on the tide. 

And as the beam cut through the dark, Silas raised his mug of tea to the invisible horizon, whispering into the salt air: *"I remember you, Clara."*
